content: Cefditoren is typically prescribed at a dose of 200 mg orally once daily. For end-stage conditions, specific dosing guidelines have not been established. It is recommended to take this medication with food to enhance absorption. Cefditoren is effective against infections caused by Haemophilus influenzae, Haemophilus parainfluenzae, Streptococcus pneumoniae, and Moraxella catarrhalis. It is also used for pharyngitis or tonsillitis caused by Streptococcus pyogenes and skin infections caused by Staphylococcus aureus and Streptococcus pyogenes. However, its safety and efficacy in children under 12 years of age have not been established, while dosing for those over 12 years is the same as for adults. Cefditoren interacts with several medications and substances. It reduces the effectiveness of live bacterial vaccines, such as the BCG vaccine, due to pharmacodynamic antagonism. Live bacterial vaccines should not be administered until antibiotic therapy is completed. Similarly, the cholera vaccine should not be given within 14 days of antibiotic use, as antibiotics may inactivate the vaccine strain. Cefditoren also interacts with oral microbiota supplements, potentially reducing their efficacy. Antibiotic regimens should be completed 2–4 days before initiating oral microbiota therapy. Cefditoren’s absorption and effectiveness can be reduced by agents that increase gastric pH, such as aluminum hydroxide, calcium carbonate, cimetidine, famotidine, ibuprofen/famotidine, sodium bicarbonate, and sodium zirconium cyclosilicate. These interactions apply only to oral forms of both agents. It is advised to administer these drugs at least two hours apart from cefditoren. Additionally, cefditoren may alter intestinal flora, potentially reducing the effectiveness of oral contraceptives and hormone therapies like bazedoxifene/conjugated estrogens and dienogest/estradiol valerate. While the risk of contraceptive failure is low, alternative or additional birth control methods may be advisable during concurrent use. Cefditoren increases the toxicity of aminoglycosides, such as amikacin, gentamicin, kanamycin, neomycin, plazomicin, streptomycin, and tobramycin, by enhancing nephrotoxic and/or ototoxic effects. Caution and close monitoring are recommended when co-administering these drugs. Similarly, co-administration with voclosporin may increase the risk of nephrotoxicity. Cefditoren may also increase the effects of warfarin, necessitating careful monitoring of coagulation parameters. Cefditoren’s bactericidal activity may be inhibited by bacteriostatic agents, such as azithromycin, clarithromycin, doxycycline, erythromycin (in various forms), minocycline, tetracycline, and demeclocycline. These interactions occur due to pharmacodynamic antagonism, and caution is advised when using these agents together. Additionally, cefditoren may interfere with the therapeutic effects of immune checkpoint inhibitors, such as atezolizumab, avelumab, balstilimab, camrelizumab, cemiplimab, dostarlimab, durvalumab, nivolumab, pembrolizumab, penpulimab, retifanlimab, sintilimab, tislelizumab, and toripalimab. Close monitoring is recommended in these cases. Cefditoren may cause gastrointestinal side effects, including diarrhea (11–15%), nausea (4–6%), abdominal pain (2%), dyspepsia (1–2%), and vomiting (1%). Other potential adverse effects include headache (2–3%), hypersensitivity reactions, increased bleeding time, vaginal yeast infections, bacterial or fungal superinfections, and Clostridioides difficile colitis. Rarely, it may cause Stevens-Johnson syndrome. Prolonged use may lead to the emergence of resistant organisms or carnitine deficiency, particularly in individuals with predisposing conditions. Patients with documented hypersensitivity to cefditoren, penicillin, related compounds, or milk protein (sodium caseinate) should avoid this medication. Caution is advised in breastfeeding, as excretion in breast milk is unknown. Cefditoren is a semi-synthetic cephalosporin prodrug that is hydrolyzed by esterases during absorption, becoming active in the bloodstream. Its bactericidal activity results from inhibition of bacterial cell wall synthesis by binding to penicillin-binding proteins. The drug is primarily excreted in the urine, with a half-life of 1.5–3 hours. It is generally considered safe during pregnancy (Category B), with no evidence of fetal risk in controlled studies.
